text.p: Grupo Financiero Bancomer is expected to report limp earnings of $0.18 per ADR in the first quarter, or about seven centavos per share, according to a survey of five banking analysts.

The profit, estimated by one analyst as a net gain of 450 million pesos, would compare with a 1.865 billion peso loss in Q1 1996, when the bank created extraordinary loan-loss provisions, but would be short of the 1.015 billion peso profit last quarter.

This quarter, like all Mexican banks, Bancomer will report under new U.S. GAAP accounting standards, which are expected to put additional pressure on net interest margins, though opinions vary on how much.
Where analysts say it may suffer worse than its main rival Banamex-Accival (Banacci) is in asset quality.

"Bancomer's lower capitalization makes it more vulnerable to asset quality deterioration, since it does not have a comfortable capital cushion to create reserves," said Carlos Gomez, Latin American bank analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.
He expected a $450 million peso net profit, or seven centavos per share, spot on the Reuters consensus.

In a report, he expected to see some asset quality deterioration due to changes in the definition of past-due mortgages, which he said would cause Bancomer to create some 650 million pesos of reserves in the three-month period.
He also said he would watch out for any announcement on how the bank, Mexico's second largest, will meet its $500 million capitalization commitment for 1997.
ING Barings analyst Petru Vaduva forecast a $0.31 per ADR or 0.12 pesos per share profit, the highest forecast but one he described as "more a stabilization than a dramatic recovery.
"Considering the still-significant amount of equity exposed to unreserved past-due loans and the group's low profitability, we believe it is too early to expect a recovery," he wrote in a report.

He expected loan growth to remain minimal, and continued pressure on net interest income, partly due to the squeezing of its net interest margin which has been hit by "waves of loan restructuring and higher cost of financing."

But he said some of the bad news may be offset by an improvement in non-interest income and what he expected to be a substantial decline in loan loss provisioning -- with a ratio of past-due loans to total loans of 17.8 percent and reserve coverage of around 58 percent.

Some analysts said the net interest margin -- which according to two estimates fell to 6.1 percent in Q4 -- would drop more than at Banamex, because the latter bank has already taken more of a hit in the past.
"GFB carries on a relative basis more restructured loans (than Banamex) and the yields are not quite as attractive," said Robert Lacoursiere of Santander Investment.
Most analysts expected the bank to use tax credits to buttress its earnings performance.
